questions.why: The reflexive pronoun sits before the verb and matches the subject; the verb itself conjugates normally, so lever keeps its è in the silent-ending forms.
Nous nous lavons is not a typo: the first nous is the subject, the second is the reflexive pronoun.
Te elides to t' before a vowel, and appeler doubles its l where the ending is silent: je m'appelle, tu t'appelles.
Before an infinitive the reflexive pronoun still matches the subject; it is not frozen as se. Je vais me lever, tu vas te lever, nous allons nous lever.

questions.q: Build the sentence: I don't get up early.
questions.why: Ne wraps the pronoun and the verb together: ne me lève pas. The reflexive pronoun never escapes outside the ne … pas sandwich.

questions.q: How do you tell someone (tu) to get up?
questions.why: In a positive command the pronoun moves after the verb and te becomes toi. The negative command puts it back in front: Ne te lève pas !

questions.q: Negative command (tu, se lever): Ne ___ pas !
questions.why: Only the positive command moves the pronoun behind the verb. A negative command restores the normal order, and toi reverts to te.
Se passer is idiomatic: passer means to pass, se passer means to happen. In this group the pronoun no longer means self at all.
Se demander is idiomatic: demander is to ask, se demander is to wonder. The pronoun no longer means self.

choices: Je me rappelle de cette journée.
Je me souviens de cette journée.
questions.why: Se souvenir takes de; se rappeler takes a direct object with no preposition. Je me rappelle de is common in speech and still wrong in writing.
All reflexives take être, and here se is the direct object, so the participle agrees with the subject: lavée.

questions.q: Passé composé: Elle (se laver) ___ les mains.
questions.why: Les mains is the direct object, which makes se merely indirect, so nothing agrees. Same for elle s'est cassé la jambe.

questions.q: Build the sentence: We didn't wash.
questions.why: In a compound tense ne … pas wraps the auxiliary, with the reflexive pronoun tucked in before it: ne nous sommes pas lavés.

questions.q: Say this out loud: we get up early.
questions.why: Both nous really are said. The doubled pronoun is the shape learners most often clip, and dropping one makes the sentence ungrammatical.

questions.q: Name the four jobs a reflexive verb can do, with an example of each.
a: 1. Genuinely reflexive: Je me lave. 2. Reciprocal, to each other: Ils se parlent. 3. Idiomatic, the meaning shifts: Qu'est-ce qui se passe ? 4. Instead of a passive: Le vin blanc se boit frais.
questions.why: Only the first job matches the English idea of self; the idiomatic group is the biggest, and the passive-replacement use is the one English speakers never predict.

questions.q: Build the sentence: I'm going to get up early.
questions.why: The reflexive pronoun agrees with the subject and travels with the infinitive: me lever, not se lever.

questions.q: Build the positive command: Get up! (tu)
questions.why: In a positive command the pronoun follows the verb and te becomes toi. The negative goes back to normal: ne te lève pas.
